unit.title: Produce management reports to enable effective decision making

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: An accountant is asked to produce a new monthly report for the general manager of a Negril hotel. What should she do first?
options: Copy the layout of the hotel's annual financial statements
Ask the manager which decisions the report must support
Include every figure the accounting system can produce
Choose the colours and charts the report will use

questions.stem: How do management reports mainly differ from the financial statements a company publishes each year?
options: They follow a fixed legal format set out in company law
They are written mainly for shareholders and the tax authority
They are shaped to help managers plan, control and decide
They are produced only once a year after the audit is complete

questions.stem: A supermarket chain's store managers and its board both need sales reports. Which approach is best?
options: Store managers get daily detail; the board gets a monthly summary
Both get the same 40-page report so nobody misses anything
The board gets daily detail; store managers get a yearly summary
Neither gets sales figures, only the cost figures for the month

questions.stem: A report that shows managers only the items outside agreed limits, such as costs more than 5% over budget, is known as what?
options: A trial balance
An internal audit report
A cash book
An exception report

questions.stem: The finance director asks for a one-off report on whether to open a new branch in Mandeville. What kind of report is this?
options: A routine monthly report
An ad hoc decision report
A statutory annual return
A daily flash sales report

questions.stem: Which report would best help a credit manager decide which customers to chase for payment this week?
options: An aged receivables report
A register of fixed assets
A monthly payroll summary
A budget for next year

questions.stem: Before sending a decision report, an accountant notices that the sales total in it differs from the general ledger by J$350,000. What should she do?
options: Send the report and explain the gap next month
Change the ledger so it agrees with the report
Find and fix the cause before the report is sent
Remove the sales total from the report this time

questions.stem: Which control best helps make sure the cost figures used in a decision report are reliable?
options: Asking the manager who will read it whether it looks right
Rounding every figure to the nearest million dollars
Producing the report as quickly as possible each time
Tracing the key figures back to the accounting records

questions.stem: A report uses sales data from the till system and cost data from the accounting system. Why must the two cover the same period?
options: So the figures can be compared and margins are correct
So the report can be printed on fewer pages each month
So the tax authority will accept the report as filed
So the managers do not have to read the cost figures

questions.stem: Halfway through the year, one branch changed the way it codes its costs. A report compares this year's branch costs with last year's. What should the report do?
options: Compare the figures as they are and say nothing about it
Leave that branch out of the comparison for the whole year
Restate the figures on one basis, or clearly note the change
Ask the branch to change its coding back before the report goes out

questions.stem: A firm has already spent J$2,000,000 on a feasibility study for a new product. When deciding whether to launch the product, how should this J$2,000,000 be treated?
options: Added to the launch cost, as it is a real cost
Ignored, as it is a sunk cost that will not change
Spread over the first year of the product's sales
Used to raise the selling price of the product

questions.stem: A Spanish Town firm owns a warehouse that it could rent out for J$300,000 a month. Instead it plans to use the space for a new project. What is the relevant cost of the space for the project?
options: Nil, because the firm already owns the warehouse
The warehouse's original purchase price
J$300,000 a month, the rent given up
The warehouse's monthly depreciation charge

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a relevant cost for a decision?
options: Any cost shown in last year's financial statements
A future cash cost that changes with the decision
A fixed overhead shared out across all departments
A cost that has already been paid in the past

questions.stem: A factory makes a part at a variable cost of J$420 a unit. Its fixed costs will not change whether it makes or buys. A supplier offers the part at J$470. For 10,000 units, what is the effect of buying instead of making?
options: Profit rises by J$500,000
Profit falls by J$4,700,000
Profit is unchanged
Profit falls by J$500,000

questions.stem: Apart from cost, which factor should a make-or-buy report also point out to managers?
options: The supplier's reliability and control over quality
The colour of the supplier's delivery vans
How long the factory building has been owned
The number of directors on the firm's board

questions.stem: A hotel kitchen with spare capacity is offered a one-off order for 400 conference meals at J$1,500 each. The variable cost per meal is J$1,150 and fixed costs will not change. What is the effect on profit?
options: A loss of J$140,000
A gain of J$600,000
A gain of J$140,000
A gain of J$460,000

questions.stem: When reporting on a special order priced below the normal selling price, what risk should the report mention?
options: Fixed costs will rise because of the special order
Regular customers may ask for the same lower price
The order will use no materials or labour at all
The firm's bank will refuse to accept the payment

questions.stem: Machine time is limited. Product A earns a contribution of J$600 and uses 2 machine hours. Product B earns J$900 and uses 4 machine hours. Which should get priority, and why?
options: B, because its contribution per unit is J$300 higher
B, because it uses more of the machine's time
Either, because both have positive contribution
A, because it earns J$300 per hour against J$225

questions.stem: A branch shows a contribution of J$1,200,000 and its own fixed costs of J$900,000. It is also charged J$500,000 of head office costs that will continue if it closes. If the branch closes, what happens to the company's profit?
options: It falls by J$300,000
It rises by J$200,000
It rises by J$500,000
It is unchanged

questions.stem: Why can a report that charges shared head office costs to each branch mislead managers deciding whether to close a branch?
options: Shared costs are always charged twice in such reports
Shared costs may stay even if the branch closes
Shared costs are not real costs for the business
Shared costs are only paid in the final month

questions.stem: A product sells for J$800 and has a variable cost of J$560. What is its contribution-to-sales ratio?

A consulting firm's engineers are fully booked on client work that earns a contribution of J$6,000 an hour after their pay. An internal project needs 50 engineer hours, and their pay of J$2,500 an hour will be paid either way. What is the relevant cost of the hours for the project?
options: Nil

questions.stem: Project X is expected to earn a yearly profit of J$1,200,000 on capital of J$8,000,000. Project Y is expected to earn J$900,000 on capital of J$5,000,000. Which statement is correct?
options: X gives the better return, because its yearly profit is J$300,000 higher
Both give the same return on the capital used
X gives 15% and Y gives 12%, so X is better
Y gives 18% against 15% for X, so Y uses capital better

questions.stem: A distributor holds inventory of J$1,500,000. Its cost of sales for the year is J$9,125,000. Using a 365-day year, about how many days of inventory does it hold?
options: 45 days
60 days
75 days
90 days

questions.stem: A restaurant plans to cut a meal's price from J$2,000 to J$1,800, expecting monthly sales to rise from 1,000 to 1,200 meals. The variable cost is J$1,200 a meal. What is the effect on monthly contribution?
options: It falls by J$80,000
It rises by J$160,000
It rises by J$40,000
It is unchanged

questions.stem: A report shows gross margin fell from 38% to 31% while sales rose. Which is the most likely explanation to investigate first?
options: Office rent rose during the year
Cost of goods rose or prices were cut
More staff took annual leave this year
The firm paid more interest on its loan

questions.stem: An exception report shows overtime at the Ocho Rios branch was 40% over budget last month. What should the report writer add before sending it?
options: A recommendation to discipline the branch manager at the next meeting
A copy of every overtime claim made during the month
The likely cause, such as extra trade or absence, and its effect
Nothing more, since the figure speaks clearly for itself

questions.stem: A report shows that sales value rose by 15% while the number of units sold rose by only 2%. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The firm sold far fewer units than last year
Variable costs per unit fell sharply
Fixed costs were spread over more units
Prices rose or customers bought dearer items

questions.stem: A company's results look strong compared with last year. Why should the report also compare them with the budget or with similar firms?
options: Last year may have been unusually weak, so the gain may mislead
Budgets are always more accurate than actual results
Similar firms' figures are always better than one's own
Comparing with last year is not allowed in reports

questions.stem: The electricity budget for a quarter was J$850,000. Actual spending was J$935,000. How should the report show the variance?
options: J$85,000 favourable, 10% under budget
J$85,000 adverse, 10% over budget
J$93,500 adverse, 11% over budget
J$85,000 adverse, 9% under budget

questions.stem: A hotel spent J$1,350,000 on laundry in a month in which it sold 9,000 room-nights. What was the laundry cost per room-night?
A courier firm is deciding whether to add a night shift. Which information is most relevant to the decision report?
options: Extra contribution from more deliveries against the shift's extra costs
The total cost of the head office building over the past ten years
The number of deliveries made by each driver in the year 2015
The share of the firm's fixed costs already charged to each depot this year

questions.stem: What should the recommendation section of a decision report contain?
options: A full copy of every working paper used in preparing the report
A list of every option the writer thought of but did not test
The preferred option, the reasons for it and the next steps
A summary of the history of the business since it was founded

questions.stem: A dashboard uses red, amber and green to show performance. Why should it also show the actual figures and the target?
options: So that the dashboard can be printed in black and white
So readers see how far off target each measure is
So that the colours can be changed by each reader
So that the report is longer and looks more complete

questions.stem: Which chart best shows whether branches that spend more on advertising also have higher sales, across 20 branches?
options: A pie chart
A scatter chart
A Gantt chart
An organisation chart

questions.stem: Which chart is best for showing each product's share of total sales in one month?
options: A line chart
A scatter chart
A Gantt chart
A pie chart

questions.stem: Where should the main findings and recommendations of a management report usually appear?
options: In an executive summary at the start
Only in the appendix at the end
Scattered through the tables
In a separate email sent weeks later

questions.stem: A busy managing director says a decision report is too long to read before the board meeting. What is the best change?
options: Print it in smaller type so that it uses fewer pages each month
Withdraw it until she asks for it again
Lead with a one-page summary and move detail to appendices
Send it to her twice so that she does not miss it

questions.stem: A forecast in a report assumes that the exchange rate will stay the same for a year. What should the report do?
options: Hide the assumption so the forecast looks certain
State the assumption and show what happens if it changes
Remove all figures that depend on the exchange rate
Use a different rate for each month without saying why

questions.stem: What does sensitivity analysis show in a decision report?
options: How the result changes if key figures differ from the estimate
Which managers are most sensitive to criticism of the plan
The order in which the report's sections should be read
The number of errors found in last month's report

questions.stem: A report shows that closing a rural branch would save money. Which other factor should it also raise for the decision-makers?
options: The colour scheme used in the branch
The age of the branch's computers
The effect on customers, staff and the firm's name
The number of windows in the building

questions.stem: A report on planned job cuts is still being drafted. A staff member asks the accountant who will be affected. What should she do?
options: Tell the staff member, since he will find out anyway
Show him the draft in private if he promises not to tell
Hint at the answer without naming any person directly
Keep it confidential and refer him to the proper manager

questions.stem: A manager asks the analyst to show only the figures that favour the option he prefers in a decision report. What should the analyst do?
options: Do as asked, since the manager will make the final decision
Present all the options and relevant figures fairly
Show the other options in an appendix that few will read
Remove the figures for every option to avoid any argument

questions.stem: A decision report on a possible purchase of a rival firm contains highly sensitive information. How should it be handled?
options: Share it only with named readers, marked confidential and protected
Email it to all managers in the firm so that they can prepare for the change
Print extra copies and leave them in the boardroom for the week
Send a summary of it to the firm's suppliers and main customers

questions.stem: Some months after a decision based on a report, why should the accountant compare the actual results with the report's forecast?
options: To show the board that the decision cannot now be changed
To find which member of staff should be blamed if the results were poor
To replace the need for any forecasts in future reports
To learn how accurate the forecast was and improve future reports

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What two-word term names a cost that has already been spent and cannot be changed by a decision?
What two-word term names the benefit given up when one option is chosen instead of the next best one?
What two-word term names a future cash cost that changes as a result of a decision?
What two-word term names a scarce resource, such as machine hours, that limits how much a business can produce?
Selling price is J$2,000 a unit and variable cost is J$1,400 a unit. What is the contribution per unit, in J$?
A product sells for J$500 and its variable cost is J$300. What is its contribution-to-sales ratio, as a percentage?
A firm with spare capacity accepts a one-off order for 300 units at J$900 each. The variable cost is J$700 a unit and fixed costs do not change. By how much does profit rise, in J$?
A school canteen's costs were J$2,560,000 for 16,000 meals. What was the cost per meal, in J$?
What term describes reporting that shows managers only the results that fall outside agreed limits?
What two-word Latin term describes a one-off report prepared for a particular question rather than on a regular cycle?
What two-word term names costs that stay the same in total, in the short term, whatever the level of output?
What two-word term describes testing how a result changes when key figures in a forecast are changed?
What two-word term names the short section at the start of a report that gives its main findings and recommendations?
What term names the amount by which sales revenue exceeds variable costs, before fixed costs are paid?
What two-word term names costs that rise and fall in total in direct proportion to output?

essays.stem: The board of a Mandeville agro-processor must decide whether to invest J$45,000,000 in a new juice line. Describe how you would plan and produce a management report that helps the board make this decision.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first meet the managing director to agree exactly what the board must decide, by when, and what criteria matter to it, such as return on capital, cash needs, risk and fit with the firm's strategy. I would then set out the options, including not investing and a smaller line, so the board can compare them. Next I would gather data: sales forecasts from marketing, equipment quotes, running costs from production, fruit supply prices, staffing and the cost of finance. I would use only relevant figures: future cash flows that change with the decision, leaving out sunk costs, such as the trial already paid for, and shared overheads that will not change. For each option I would show the extra contribution, cash flows and return. Because forecasts are uncertain, I would test what happens if sales or fruit prices are 10% or 20% worse. I would also set out non-financial points, such as reliable fruit supply from farmers, quality, staff skills and environmental rules. The report would open with a one-page executive summary and a clear recommendation, keep detail in appendices, and be checked by a second person before the board meeting.
markingPoints: Agrees the decision, deadline and the board's criteria first
Sets out options, including doing nothing, and gathers data from the right sources
Uses only relevant costs and cash flows, excluding sunk and unchanged costs
Tests sensitivity and covers non-financial factors
Structures the report with a summary and recommendation, and checks it before issue

essays.stem: A Kingston bakery makes 50,000 bread rolls a month. Each roll costs J$18 in materials, J$9 in labour and J$5 in variable overhead, plus J$8 of fixed overhead that will continue whatever is decided. A supplier offers rolls at J$36 each. Prepare a recommendation on whether to make or buy, with reasons.
essays.modelAnswer: The relevant cost of making a roll is the variable cost only: J$18 + J$9 + J$5 = J$32. The J$8 of fixed overhead will be paid whether the bakery makes or buys, so it is not relevant to this decision. The full cost of J$40 a roll would wrongly suggest that buying at J$36 is cheaper. Comparing relevant costs, buying costs J$4 more per roll (J$36 − J$32), which is J$4 × 50,000 = J$200,000 more each month. On cost alone, the bakery should continue to make the rolls. The report should also raise non-financial points. Making gives control over freshness and quality, which matters for a bakery's name. Buying might free space and staff for more profitable products, which would be an opportunity cost of making and could change the answer if the freed capacity earned more than J$200,000 a month. The supplier's reliability, delivery times and contract terms would also need checking. My recommendation is to continue making the rolls, unless managers have a clear, more profitable use for the capacity.
markingPoints: Calculates the relevant (variable) cost of making correctly as J$32
Explains that the J$8 fixed overhead is not relevant
Calculates that buying costs J$200,000 more a month
Raises non-financial factors: quality, control, supplier reliability
Considers the opportunity cost of freed capacity and gives a clear recommendation

essays.stem: A hardware chain's Port Antonio branch has sales of J$30,000,000, variable costs of J$21,000,000, its own fixed costs of J$7,500,000, and is charged J$2,500,000 of head office costs that will continue if it closes. The branch report shows a loss of J$1,000,000. Evaluate whether the branch should be closed.
essays.modelAnswer: The branch's contribution is J$30,000,000 − J$21,000,000 = J$9,000,000. After its own fixed costs of J$7,500,000, it earns J$1,500,000 towards head office costs. The reported loss of J$1,000,000 appears only after charging J$2,500,000 of head office costs. Since these costs will continue if the branch closes, they would be spread over the other branches. Closing the branch would therefore lower the company's total profit by J$1,500,000 a year, not raise it by J$1,000,000. On the figures alone, the branch should stay open. The report should also point out other factors. Closing would cost staff their jobs and might bring redundancy costs, and it would leave customers in Portland without a store, which could hurt the chain's name. On the other hand, if the space or money could be used for something earning more than J$1,500,000, or if the branch's sales are falling fast, closure might be right later. I would recommend keeping the branch open, and looking for ways to improve its margin, such as better stock control.
markingPoints: Calculates contribution of J$9,000,000 correctly
Shows the branch earns J$1,500,000 after its own fixed costs
Explains that head office costs continue, so closing lowers profit by J$1,500,000
Considers non-financial factors: staff, customers, reputation
Considers other uses or trends and gives a justified recommendation

essays.stem: Explain why a decision report should use only relevant costs, and illustrate your answer with examples of sunk, committed, opportunity and incremental costs from a Jamaican business.
essays.modelAnswer: A decision is about the future, so only costs and revenues that will change because of the decision should affect it. Including costs that will be the same whatever is chosen can make a good option look bad, or a poor one look good. Take a Montego Bay tour company deciding whether to start a new river tour. The J$400,000 it has already spent on a market survey is a sunk cost: it is spent whatever the company decides, so it is left out. The rent on its head office, which it must pay under a lease, is a committed cost that will not change, so it is also left out. If the company plans to use one of its own buses for the new tour, and that bus could otherwise be hired out to a hotel for J$80,000 a week, the J$80,000 given up is an opportunity cost and must be included. The extra fuel, guide wages, insurance and park fees that arise only if the tour runs are incremental costs and are included. The report should show these relevant figures clearly, and explain in a note why the others were left out, so managers are not confused.
markingPoints: Explains that decisions concern the future, so only changing costs count
Explains and illustrates a sunk cost correctly
Explains and illustrates a committed cost correctly
Explains and illustrates an opportunity cost correctly
Explains and illustrates incremental costs, and notes how the report should show them

essays.stem: A Kingston restaurant is thinking of cutting the price of its lunch special from J$1,500 to J$1,350, expecting meals sold to rise from 2,000 to 2,500 a month. The variable cost is J$900 a meal. Evaluate the proposal and recommend what the owner should do.
essays.modelAnswer: At present each meal earns a contribution of J$1,500 − J$900 = J$600, so 2,000 meals earn J$1,200,000 a month. After the cut, each meal would earn J$1,350 − J$900 = J$450, so 2,500 meals would earn J$1,125,000. Although sales revenue would rise, contribution would fall by J$75,000 a month. To keep the same contribution at the lower price, the restaurant would need to sell J$1,200,000 ÷ J$450 = about 2,667 meals, a rise of about 33%, not 25%. The report should also check other points. Can the kitchen and staff serve 500 or more extra meals at lunchtime without overtime, which would raise costs further? Is the forecast of 2,500 meals based on evidence, such as a trial, or a guess? Will customers who already pay J$1,500 simply pay less? On the other hand, a lower price might bring new customers who also buy drinks or return for dinner, which the figures do not show. My recommendation is not to cut the price on present figures, but to run a short trial, for example on two days a week, and measure the extra meals and other sales before deciding.
markingPoints: Calculates present contribution of J$1,200,000 correctly
Calculates new contribution of J$1,125,000 and the fall of J$75,000
Works out the volume needed to keep contribution (about 2,667 meals)
Considers capacity, the reliability of the forecast and wider effects
Gives a clear, justified recommendation, such as a trial

essays.stem: Compare a one-page dashboard with a full written report as ways of giving information to senior managers, and recommend how a medium-sized firm should use them.
essays.modelAnswer: A dashboard shows a small number of key measures on one page or screen, often with charts and red, amber and green signals against targets. Its strengths are that managers can see the position and spot problems in seconds, it can be updated often, even daily, and it focuses attention on what matters most. Its weaknesses are that it gives little explanation of why results have changed, colours can hide how far off target a measure is, and a poorly chosen set of measures can give a false picture. A full written report gives detailed figures, explanations, analysis of causes, assumptions and recommendations. It supports careful decisions and leaves a record. However, it takes longer to prepare and to read, and busy managers may skip it, missing important points. I would recommend that the firm uses both together. A dashboard of eight to twelve key measures, with actual figures and targets as well as colours, should be updated weekly or monthly to show the position at a glance. Written reports should then explain the main changes, analyse problems and set out options and recommendations when a decision is needed, with detail in appendices for those who need it.
markingPoints: Describes a dashboard and its strengths
Notes the weaknesses of a dashboard
Describes a written report and its strengths
Notes the weaknesses of a written report
Recommends using both, with a sensible design for each

essays.stem: A Montego Bay garment maker with spare capacity is offered a one-off order for 2,000 shirts at J$1,600 each. Its normal price is J$2,200 and the variable cost is J$1,250 a shirt. Fixed costs will not change. Prepare a recommendation for the managing director.
essays.modelAnswer: Because the firm has spare capacity and fixed costs will not change, the relevant figures are the price and the variable cost. Each shirt earns a contribution of J$1,600 − J$1,250 = J$350. On 2,000 shirts, the order adds J$350 × 2,000 = J$700,000 to profit. On the figures alone, the order should be accepted. However, the report must also raise other points. If regular customers learn of the lower price, they may demand the same, which could cost far more than J$700,000. The firm should check that the order truly fits within spare capacity, as overtime or extra staff would raise the cost. It should also confirm that the buyer is creditworthy, that the delivery date is realistic and that quality can be kept. A one-off order may also lead to future work, which is a benefit, but the firm must not get used to selling below its normal price. I recommend accepting the order, provided it is kept separate from normal customers, for example under a different label, and the capacity and credit checks are satisfactory.
markingPoints: Calculates contribution of J$350 per shirt correctly
Calculates the total gain of J$700,000 correctly
Raises the risk to normal prices and customers
Checks capacity, credit, delivery and quality
Gives a clear recommendation with conditions

essays.stem: A St Catherine plastics firm has only 2,000 machine hours a month. Product P earns a contribution of J$1,200 a unit and uses 3 hours; Q earns J$1,500 and uses 5 hours; R earns J$800 and uses 1 hour. Monthly demand is 300 P, 200 Q and 500 R. Recommend a production plan and explain your method.
essays.modelAnswer: Demand needs 900 hours for P (300 × 3), 1,000 for Q (200 × 5) and 500 for R (500 × 1), a total of 2,400 hours, so machine time is the limiting factor. The firm should rank products by contribution per machine hour, not per unit. P earns J$1,200 ÷ 3 = J$400 an hour, Q earns J$1,500 ÷ 5 = J$300 an hour and R earns J$800 ÷ 1 = J$800 an hour. The order is R, then P, then Q. Making all 500 R uses 500 hours, and all 300 P uses 900 hours, leaving 600 hours for Q, enough for 120 units. Contribution would be R J$400,000, P J$360,000 and Q J$180,000, a total of J$940,000 a month. If the firm had ranked by contribution per unit, it would make Q first and earn only J$740,000, so the method matters. The report should also note other points: if Q is bought by a key customer who also buys other products, cutting its supply could cost more than the figures show. Managers might also consider overtime, a second shift or outsourcing Q if the extra contribution covers the extra cost.
markingPoints: Shows that demand needs 2,400 hours, so machine time limits output
Calculates contribution per machine hour for each product correctly
Ranks R, P, Q and allocates hours to give 500 R, 300 P and 120 Q
Calculates the total contribution of J$940,000 correctly
Raises customer or capacity factors that could change the plan

essays.stem: Discuss the ethical and confidentiality duties of a person who produces management reports, and explain how they should respond to pressure to present figures in a misleading way.
essays.modelAnswer: A person who produces management reports must be honest and objective. The figures must be accurate and complete, and the report must not hide losses, delay bad news, leave out options that a manager dislikes or present estimates as facts. Assumptions and limits should be stated so readers are not misled. Reports often contain sensitive information, such as salaries, plans for job cuts, pricing or customer details, so they must be shared only with authorised readers, stored securely and sent by protected means. Personal data must be handled in line with the data protection law. The writer must also avoid conflicts of interest, such as shaping figures to make their own department look good. If a manager presses them to leave out a loss or to change figures, they should calmly explain that the report must be accurate and offer to include an explanation or recovery plan instead. They should keep a record of the request. If the pressure continues, they should raise it with a more senior manager, the finance director or internal audit, using the firm's reporting or whistle-blowing policy. They should never sign or send a report they know is misleading.
markingPoints: Explains the duty of accuracy, completeness and honesty, including stated assumptions
Explains confidentiality of sensitive information and secure distribution
Mentions data protection or conflicts of interest
Describes refusing calmly, offering an honest alternative and keeping a record
Describes escalating through proper channels and never sending a misleading report

essays.stem: A report recommends opening a new branch based on a forecast of sales, costs and the exchange rate. Explain how the report should deal with assumptions and uncertainty so that managers can make a sound decision.
essays.modelAnswer: Every forecast depends on assumptions, and managers need to know what they are. The report should list the key assumptions clearly, such as expected sales in the first year, the selling price, rent, staff numbers and the exchange rate for imported stock, and say where each came from, for example market research or supplier quotes. It should then show how sensitive the result is to changes in these figures. Sensitivity analysis could show the profit if sales are 10% or 20% lower than forecast, or if the Jamaican dollar weakens against the US dollar. The report could present three scenarios: expected, pessimistic and optimistic. It could also show the level of sales at which the branch would just cover its costs, so managers know how far sales could fall before it makes a loss. The report should identify the main risks and ways to reduce them, such as a shorter first lease or a phased opening. Finally, it should state the limits of the analysis honestly. This lets managers see the range of possible results and decide how much risk they are willing to accept, rather than relying on one figure that may prove wrong.
markingPoints: Lists key assumptions and their sources
Uses sensitivity analysis on the main figures
Presents scenarios or the sales level at which costs are just covered
Identifies risks and ways to reduce them
States the limits honestly so managers can judge the risk

practical1.title: Produce a product-line profitability report and recommend which lines to keep, reprice or drop
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a spreadsheet for a made-up Jamaican manufacturer (for example a St Thomas food processor with six product lines such as sauces, jams and juices): sales and variable costs for each line, fixed costs that belong to each line, shared overheads charged to each line, machine hours used, the hours available and notes on customers and suppliers. The managing director (played by the assessor) wants to know which lines to keep, reprice or drop. Give each member a named role: report lead (agrees the decision and criteria with the managing director and writes the executive summary and recommendation), data checker (reconciles the spreadsheet totals to the control totals given and records any problems), contribution analyst (calculates contribution and profit before shared overheads for each line, checking every figure twice), limiting factor analyst (calculates contribution per machine hour, ranks the lines and shows the best mix within the hours available), and non-financial reviewer (lists the customer, staff, supplier and reputation points for each line that is at risk). In a group of four, the report lead also does the non-financial review. Write a report of no more than four pages plus appendices, and present it to the managing director in 10 minutes.
materials: Data spreadsheet, control totals and case notes from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word processor software
photos: The notes from the meeting with the managing director on the decision and criteria
The data checker's reconciliation of the totals
The spreadsheet on screen showing contribution and profit before shared overheads for each line
The ranking by contribution per machine hour and the proposed product mix
The executive summary and recommendation, and the group presenting
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the report
Reconciled the data to the control totals and recorded any differences
Contribution and profit before shared overheads are correct and were checked twice
Treated shared overheads correctly and did not drop a line only because of them
Ranked lines by contribution per machine hour and built a mix within the hours available
Weighed non-financial points in the recommendation
Presented clearly and answered the managing director's questions
safety: Treat the case data as confidential business information; do not copy it to personal devices
Hand all printouts to the assessor at the end and delete working files as the assessor directs
Respect each other's views; challenge ideas, not people
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Prepare and present a decision report to a management panel
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a decision case for a made-up Jamaican business, with figures (for example a food processor in Clarendon deciding whether to keep making its own bottles or buy them in, or a hotel deciding whether to accept a large conference booking at a reduced rate). As a group, prepare a decision report and present it to a management panel played by the assessor and one other person. Give each member a named role: lead writer (writes the purpose, background and executive summary), cost analyst (sorts the costs into relevant and not relevant, and calculates the financial effect of each option, checking every figure twice), sensitivity analyst (tests how the result changes if two key figures change by 10% and 20%, and presents the results in a small table or chart), risk and non-financial reviewer (lists the non-financial factors, such as quality, staff, customers and supplier reliability, with their effect on the decision), and presenter (prepares four to six slides or flipchart pages and leads the presentation). In a group of four, the lead writer also presents. The report gives a clear recommendation. The presentation lasts 10 minutes, followed by 5 minutes of questions in which every member answers at least one question.
materials: Decision case with figures from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet, word processor and presentation software
Projector or screen, or flipchart paper and markers
photos: The cost analysis showing relevant and non-relevant costs for each option
The written decision report with its executive summary and recommendation
The slides or flipchart pages and the group presenting
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the report
Correctly separated relevant from non-relevant (sunk or unchanged) costs
Financial effect of each option is calculated correctly and checked twice
Sensitivity analysis is correct and its meaning is explained
Non-financial factors are relevant and weighed in the recommendation
Recommendation is clear and justified by the analysis
safety: Treat the case figures as confidential; hand in all printouts at the end
Use only the made-up business; do not use real firms' figures
Respect each other's views; challenge ideas, not people
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks
